title: Just now
description: Say how long ago something happened.
grammarNote: Acabar de plus an infinitive means to have just done something: acabar de comer.

explanation.summary: Spanish has two ways to talk about the recent past, and one of them is an idiom rather than a verb form. Acabar de plus an infinitive means to have just done something.

sections.heading: Acabar de
sections.body: The verb acabar means to finish, and the phrase acabar de plus an infinitive means to have just done that thing: acabo de llegar, I have just arrived. It is the everyday way to say something happened a moment ago, and it works with any verb: acabo de comer, I have just eaten.

examples.en: He has just finished the film.

sections.heading: Hace, ago
sections.body: Hace plus a time means how long ago: hace dos horas, two hours ago; hace una semana, a week ago. The verb is hacer and the phrase works with a period. Yesterday is ayer, and just now is recién.

examples.en: I saw it two hours ago.

sections.heading: Since, for
sections.body: Desde says since, and for how long something has lasted: desde enero, since January; desde hace dos años, for two years. The phrase desde hace is fixed, and it is the way to say for in this sense.

examples.en: I have lived in Madrid since January.

examples.es: Estudio español desde hace dos años.
examples.en: I have studied Spanish for two years.

examples.es: Desde que llegué, no he salido.
examples.en: Since I arrived, I have not gone out.

items.note: Acabar de plus an infinitive means to have just done it.
Ago. Make hace dos horas, hace un año.
A little while ago. It is often used with acabar de.
Last, as in el pasado año. It also means passed.
Before, earlier. Antes de plus an infinitive.
During. It goes with a period: durante el viaje.

drills.meaning: I saw it two hours ago
I have lived in Madrid since January
I have studied Spanish for two years
